questions.question_text: Which of these expressions is a polynomial?

options.why: Assumed roots of $x$ are allowed, but $\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{1}{2}}$ gives a fractional index.
Assumed $x$ in a denominator is allowed, but $\frac{4}{x}=4x^{-1}$ gives a negative index.
In $3^{x}$ the variable sits in the index, so the term is not of the form $ax^{n}$ with a whole-number index.

questions.solution_text:
$2x^{3}-x+9$
Every index of $x$ is a whole number ($3$, $1$ and $0$), so it is a polynomial.

questions.question_text: The polynomial $9x-x^{3}+2$ is best described as:

options.why: Named from the first term written, $9x$, instead of the term with the highest index.
Counted the three terms rather than finding the highest index of $x$.
Named from the constant $+2$ at the end instead of the highest index.
Took the index of the first $x$-term written instead of the highest index.
Gave the size of the leading coefficient rather than the highest index.
Counted the number of terms instead of finding the highest index.
Took the coefficient of the first term written, but the leading term is the one with the highest index.
Gave the index of the leading term instead of its coefficient.
Gave the constant term instead of the leading coefficient.

questions.solution_text:
$4x^{2}+9x^{6}-3$
The leading term is $9x^{6}$.
Leading coefficient $9$.

options.why: Dropped the negative sign attached to the constant term.
Gave the coefficient of $x$, but the constant term is the term with no $x$ at all.
Gave the leading coefficient instead of the constant term.

questions.solution_text:
$2x^{3}-8x-6$
The term with no $x$ is $-6$.
Constant term $-6$.

questions.question_text: Which of these polynomials is monic?

options.why: A constant term of $1$ does not make a polynomial monic; the leading coefficient here is $2$.
Its leading coefficient is $5$; a monic polynomial needs a leading coefficient of exactly $1$.
$4=4x^{0}$, so its leading coefficient is $4$, not $1$.

questions.solution_text:
$x^{5}+6x-2$
Its leading term is $x^{5}$, with coefficient $1$.
Monic.

options.text: Yes — every index of $x$ is a whole number
No — a polynomial cannot contain fractions
options.why: Fractional coefficients such as $\frac{1}{7}$ are allowed; only the indices of $x$ must be whole numbers.

options.text: No — dividing by $7$ creates a negative index
options.why: Dividing by the number $7$ leaves the index of $x$ unchanged; only dividing by $x$ produces a negative index.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{x^{3}}{7}+x$
$=\frac{1}{7}x^{3}+x$
The coefficient $\frac{1}{7}$ is a real number and the indices $3$ and $1$ are whole numbers, so it is a polynomial.

options.why: Dropped the negative sign; the whole term $-x^{4}$, including its sign, is the leading term.
Took the first term written instead of the term with the highest index.
Gave the constant term rather than the term with the highest index.

questions.solution_text:
$5x-x^{4}+3x^{2}+8$
The highest index is $4$, and that term is $-x^{4}$.
Leading term $-x^{4}$.

options.text: It is a non-monic polynomial of degree $6$
It is a monic polynomial of degree $6$
options.why: The leading coefficient is $\frac{2}{5}$, not $1$, so it is not monic.

options.text: It is a non-monic polynomial of degree $2$
options.why: The degree comes from the highest index, $6$, not from the $-x^{2}$ term.
Dividing a term by the number $5$ keeps whole-number indices, so it is still a polynomial.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{2x^{6}}{5}-x^{2}+4$
$=\frac{2}{5}x^{6}-x^{2}+4$
Degree $6$; leading coefficient $\frac{2}{5}$, which is not $1$.
Non-monic polynomial of degree $6$.
